# Introduction

Transcription factors (TFs) are proteins that bind to cis-regulatory elements 
in promoter regions of genes and regulate their expression. 
Identifying them in a genome is useful for a variety of reasons, such as 
exploring their evolutionary history across clades and inferring 
gene regulatory networks. `r BiocStyle::Githubpkg("almeidasilvaf/tfhunter")` 
allows users to identify TFs from whole-genome protein sequences of any 
eukaryotic species and classify them into families using the 
classification scheme of [CIS-BP](https://cisbp.ccbr.utoronto.ca/). For 
plants, TFs can also be classified into families and subfamilies 
(when applicable) using the classification schemes implemented in 
[PlantTFDB](http://planttfdb.gao-lab.org/) and 
[TAPscan](https://tapscan.plantcode.cup.uni-freiburg.de/), as well as
into structure-based families, classes, and superclasses as in
Plant-TFClass. Likewise, mammalian TFs can be classified into structure-based
superclasses, classes, and families as in TFClass.
`r BiocStyle::Githubpkg("almeidasilvaf/tfhunter")` is the
successor of the Bioconductor package `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("planttfhunter")`.
As `r BiocStyle::Githubpkg("almeidasilvaf/tfhunter")` interoperates with 
core Bioconductor packages (i.e., `AAStringSet` objects as input, 
`SummarizedExperiment` objects as output), it can be easily incorporated in 
pipelines for TF identification and classification in large-scale genomic
data sets.

# Installation

You can install `r BiocStyle::Githubpkg("almeidasilvaf/tfhunter")` 
with the following code:

```{r "install", eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("tfhunter")
```

Loading package after installation:

```{r load_package, message = FALSE}
library(tfhunter)
```

# Data description

In this vignette, we will use protein sequences of TFs from the algae 
species *Galdieria sulphuraria* as an example, as its proteome is
very small. The proteome file was 
downloaded from the PLAZA Diatoms database [@osuna2020seminavis], and 
it was filtered to keep only genes with TF-related domains for 
demonstration purposes. 
The object `gsu` stores the protein sequences in an `AAStringSet` object.

```{r data}
data(gsu)
gsu
```


# Algorithm description

TF identification and classification is based on the presence of 
signature protein domains, which are identified using profile hidden Markov
models (HMMs). Currently, 5 classification schemes are available, and you 
can list them with the function `list_schemes()`:

```{r list_schemes}
list_schemes()
```

1. **CIS-BP** [@weirauch2014cisbp]: TFs from any eukaryotic species are 
identified based on the presence of DNA-binding domains (DBDs), and they 
are classified into families defined by the set of DBDs they contain. 
Each DBD corresponds to a family (e.g., 'Homeodomain'), and TFs with more 
than one type of DBD are assigned to a family named after all of them, 
sorted alphabetically and separated by ',' (e.g., 'Homeodomain,POU'). 
As in CIS-BP, DBD hits must have a per-sequence E-value <0.01 and a 
per-domain conditional E-value <0.01, and overlapping hits of different
DBDs are resolved by keeping only the most significant hit. 
This classification rule reproduces the families of all TFs in 
CIS-BP (build 3.10), and 
`r BiocStyle::Githubpkg("almeidasilvaf/tfhunter")` classifies TFs into the 
same CIS-BP families for >98% of the TFs identified by both CIS-BP 
and `r BiocStyle::Githubpkg("almeidasilvaf/tfhunter")` in species 
from diverse eukaryotic lineages (yeast, fruit fly, human, *Arabidopsis*,
*Phytophthora*, and *Dictyostelium*). Note that CIS-BP's TF collection 
also includes some manual curation steps that are not implemented here
(e.g., removal of proteins with SANT domains but no Myb domains, and 
manual curation of human TFs), so 
`r BiocStyle::Githubpkg("almeidasilvaf/tfhunter")` is expected to identify 
a few more TFs than CIS-BP.

2. **PlantTFDB** [@jin2016planttfdb]: TFs are classified into families and
subfamilies based on DNA-binding, auxiliary, and forbidden domains.

3. **TAPscan v4** [@petroll2025tapscan]: transcription-associated proteins
(TAPs), which include TFs, transcriptional regulators (TRs), and putative
TAPs (PTs), are classified in over 130 families based on rules specifying 
domains that each family should and should not have. Domain hits are 
identified using gathering thresholds and domain-specific coverage cutoffs. 

4. **Plant-TFClass** [@blancmathieu2024planttfclass]: TFs are classified
into families, classes, and superclasses based on the 3D structure of 
their DNA-binding domains. Plant-TFClass classifications are inferred from 
TAPscan classifications using a correspondence table between the two
systems. Some TAPscan families correspond to more than one Plant-TFClass
family (e.g., TAPscan's AP2 family includes Plant-TFClass's AP2, ERF/DREB, 
and RAV families). In such cases, PlantTFDB subfamilies are used to resolve 
the ambiguity, and if that is not possible (e.g., because the gene was not
classified by PlantTFDB), all possible classifications are reported, 
separated by ';'.

5. **TFClass** [@wingender2018tfclass]: TFs are classified into 
superclasses, classes, and families based on the structure of their 
DNA-binding domains. TFClass includes human TFs and their mammalian 
orthologs, and TFClass classifications are inferred from CIS-BP families
using a correspondence table between the two systems, created by 
comparing the CIS-BP families and TFClass classifications of human TFs.
This approach assigns human TFs to the same TFClass classes as TFClass
itself for >99% of the TFs. However, some CIS-BP families correspond to 
more than one TFClass family (e.g., CIS-BP's Homeodomain family includes 
TFClass families HOX, NK, Paired-related HD, and others). TFs in these 
families are assigned to a single TFClass family using human and mouse TFs
with known TFClass families as references. C2H2 zinc finger TFs are 
assigned to the family of the reference TF with which they share the 
largest fraction of amino acid 5-mers, and 
other TFs are assigned to the family whose profile HMM (built from the 
DNA-binding domains of the reference TFs) has the highest score.
TFs that cannot be assigned to a single family (mostly C2H2 zinc finger 
TFs specific to some lineages, which are not classified by TFClass) have 
all possible TFClass families separated by ';'. CIS-BP families 
that do not occur in mammals (e.g., most plant and fungal families) are 
not classified by TFClass. As TFClass is a classification of mammalian TFs,
we recommend using it only for mammals, and using CIS-BP for other 
eukaryotes (including other animals).

In all schemes, classification levels without a more specific level are 
filled with the name of the more general level. For example, PlantTFDB 
family bHLH has no subfamilies, so its subfamily is also bHLH, and 
Plant-TFClass class GRAS has no families, so its family is also GRAS.

The classification schemes are available as data sets in this package, and
you can see them below (click to expand).

<details>
<summary>CIS-BP classification scheme 
(<code>data(cisbp_scheme)</code>)</summary>

Each row represents a DBD (Pfam family) and its corresponding CIS-BP 
family.

```{r scheme_cisbp, echo = FALSE}
data(cisbp_scheme)
knitr::kable(cisbp_scheme)
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>PlantTFDB classification scheme 
(<code>data(planttfdb_scheme)</code>)</summary>

```{r scheme_planttfdb, echo = FALSE}
data(planttfdb_scheme)
knitr::kable(planttfdb_scheme)
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>TAPscan classification scheme 
(<code>data(tapscan_scheme)</code>)</summary>

Genes are assigned to a family (and subfamily, if any) if they have all
domains in column *Should* and none of the domains in column *Should_not*.
Numbers in parentheses indicate the required number of copies of a domain.

```{r scheme_tapscan, echo = FALSE}
data(tapscan_scheme)
knitr::kable(tapscan_scheme)
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Correspondence between TAPscan and Plant-TFClass 
(<code>data(planttfclass_scheme)</code>)</summary>

TAPscan families/subfamilies with multiple rows correspond to more than one
Plant-TFClass family, and the PlantTFDB subfamily of each gene (column
*PlantTFDB_subfamily*) is used to choose among them.

```{r scheme_planttfclass, echo = FALSE}
data(planttfclass_scheme)
knitr::kable(planttfclass_scheme)
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Correspondence between CIS-BP and TFClass 
(<code>data(tfclass_scheme)</code>)</summary>

CIS-BP families with multiple types of DBDs that are not in this table
are classified based on the TFClass classifications of each DBD's family.

```{r scheme_tfclass, echo = FALSE}
data(tfclass_scheme)
knitr::kable(tfclass_scheme)
```

</details>

# Identifying and classifying TFs

To identify TFs from whole-genome protein sequence data, you will use the 
function `annotate_domains()`. This function takes as input an `AAStringSet` 
object [^1] and returns a list of data frames (`PlantTFDB`, `TAPscan`, and
`CISBP`) with the protein domains used by each classification scheme.
By default, domains are annotated for all classification schemes, but you
can choose specific schemes with the argument `scheme` (e.g., 
`scheme = "CISBP"`).
The HMMER program [@finn2011hmmer] is used to scan protein 
sequences for the presence of DNA-binding protein domains, as well as
auxiliary and forbidden domains. Pre-built HMM profiles can be found in the
*extdata/* directory of this package.

[^1]: **Tip:** If you have protein sequences in a FASTA file, you can read 
them into an `AAStringSet` object with the function `readAAStringSet()` from 
the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("Biostrings")` package.

Before running `annotate_domains()`, make sure that you have
a full proteome (i.e., protein sequences encoded by all protein-coding 
genes in the genome) for a given species. 
E-values reported by HMMER depend on the number of sequences that are searched, 
so domain hits with E-values close to the thresholds may pass or fail filtering 
depending on the size of the input data set. For consistent results, run 
`annotate_domains()` on the whole proteome instead of on subsets of it
(e.g., chunks of sequences or candidate TFs only). It's also important to make 
sure that you use:

- **Only one isoform per gene.** Proteomes with all isoforms of each 
gene will result in redundant TFs, as each isoform is treated as a 
separate gene. We recommend using the translated sequences of the 
longest (or canonical/primary) transcript of each gene. Note, however, 
that some TFs could be missed if their DBDs are only present in other 
isoforms (e.g., 15 human TFs in CIS-BP have DBDs that are only detected 
in isoforms other than the longest).

- **Only proteins encoded by the primary genome assembly.** Some 
proteome files (e.g., the `pep.all` files from Ensembl) also include 
proteins encoded by alternative haplotypes and assembly patches, which are 
copies of genes in the primary assembly. For example, the human proteome in 
Ensembl includes >100 copies of TFs encoded in alternative haplotypes and 
patches, which would be identified as additional TFs.


This is how you can run `annotate_domains()` [^2]:

[^2]: **Note:** in the code chunk below, the if statement is not required.
We just added it to make sure that the function `annotate_domains()` is only
executed if HMMER is installed, to avoid problems when building this
vignette in machines that do not have HMMER installed. 

```{r identifying_tfs}
data(gsu_annotation)

# Annotate TF-related domains using a local installation of HMMER
if(hmmer_is_installed()) {
    gsu_annotation <- annotate_domains(gsu)
} 

# Take a look at the first few lines of the output
lapply(gsu_annotation, head)
```

Now that we have our TF-related domains, we can classify TFs in families 
with the function `classify_tfs()`.

```{r classifying_tfs}
# Classify TFs into families
gsu_families <- classify_tfs(gsu_annotation)

# Take a look at the output
head(gsu_families)
```

The output contains one row per gene, and genes that are not classified
by one of the schemes have `NA` in the respective columns. By default, 
`classify_tfs()` uses all classification schemes for which domain 
annotation is available. Obtaining classifications from TFClass and 
Plant-TFClass requires also classifying with CIS-BP and TAPscan, respectively.
For TFClass, `annotate_domains()` also returns the evidence used to assign
TFs to a single TFClass family (element *TFClass* of the output).

You can also obtain classifications from specific schemes using the
`scheme` argument. Of note, as TAPscan's scheme also includes 
other transcription-associated proteins (e.g., transcriptional regulators),
more genes are usually classified with TAPscan. TAP classes of each family 
(TF, TR, or PT) are indicated in the column `TAP_class`. 

```{r classifying_tfs_tapscan}
# Get TAPscan classifications only
tapscan_families <- classify_tfs(gsu_annotation, scheme = "TAPscan")
head(tapscan_families)

# Number of TFs, TRs, and PTs
table(tapscan_families$TAP_class)

# Get CIS-BP and PlantTFDB classifications
cisbp_ptfdb <- classify_tfs(gsu_annotation, scheme = c("CISBP", "PlantTFDB"))
head(cisbp_ptfdb)
```

# Counting TFs per family in multiple species at once

If you want to get TF counts per family for multiple species, you can use
the function `get_tf_counts()`. This function takes a named list of 
data frames with TF classifications for each species (as returned 
by `classify_tfs()`) as input, and it returns a `SummarizedExperiment`
object containing TF counts per family in each species, as well as species
metadata (optional). If you are not familiar with the `SummarizedExperiment`
class, you should consider checking the vignettes of the 
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")` Bioconductor package.

For real data sets, you would first identify and classify TFs in each 
species. For instance, if you have a list of `AAStringSet` objects with
the proteomes of multiple species [^3], you could run:

[^3]: **Tip:** If you have whole-genome protein sequences for multiple
species as FASTA files in a given directory, you can read them all as a list
of `AAStringSet` objects with the function `fasta2AAStringSetlist()` from
the Bioconductor package `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("syntenet")`.

```{r classify_multiple_species, eval = FALSE}
families <- lapply(proteomes, function(x) classify_tfs(annotate_domains(x)))
```

To demonstrate how `get_tf_counts()` works, we will simulate TF 
classifications for 4 species by sampling 100 random genes from 
the TF classifications we obtained above (`gsu_families`) 4 times.

```{r simulate_data_families}
set.seed(123) # for reproducibility

# Simulate 4 different species by sampling 100 random genes 
families <- list(
    Gsu1 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ],
    Gsu2 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ],
    Gsu3 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ],
    Gsu4 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ]
)
```

Now, let's also create a simulated species metadata data frame for 
each "species".

```{r simulate_data_species_metadata}
# Create simulated species metadata
species_metadata <- data.frame(
    row.names = names(families),
    Division = "Rhodophyta",
    Origin = c("US", "Belgium", "China", "Brazil")
)

species_metadata
```

You can add as many columns as you want to the species metadata data frame, 
but make sure that **species names are in row names**, and 
that `names(families)` match `rownames(species_metadata)`, 
otherwise `get_tf_counts()` will return an error. 

Now that we have a list of TF classifications and species metadata, we
can execute `get_tf_counts()`. By default, TFs are counted per CIS-BP family,
but you can choose other schemes with the argument `scheme`, and
other classification levels with the argument `level`. Possible levels 
are 'family' and 'subfamily' for PlantTFDB and TAPscan, 'superclass',
'class', and 'family' for Plant-TFClass and TFClass, and 'family' for 
CIS-BP (see column
*Levels* in the output of `list_schemes()`). 

```{r get_tf_counts}
# Get TF counts per CIS-BP family in each species
tf_counts <- get_tf_counts(families, species_metadata)

# Take a look at the SummarizedExperiment object
tf_counts

# Look at the matrix of counts: assay() function from SummarizedExperiment
SummarizedExperiment::assay(tf_counts)

# Look at the species metadata: colData() function from SummarizedExperiment
SummarizedExperiment::colData(tf_counts)
```

When counting TFs at levels below the highest level of a scheme 
(e.g., subfamilies), the `rowData` of the output contains the higher 
levels of each row, which you can use to aggregate counts. Here is an 
example with PlantTFDB subfamilies:

```{r get_tf_counts_subfamily}
# Get TF counts per PlantTFDB subfamily
subfam_counts <- get_tf_counts(
    families, scheme = "PlantTFDB", level = "subfamily"
)

# Look at the family of each subfamily
head(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(subfam_counts))
```

Since `get_tf_counts()` takes classification tables as input, you can also 
filter them before counting. For example, here is how you can get counts
of TAPscan TFs (excluding TRs and PTs) per subfamily:

```{r get_tf_counts_tapscan}
# Keep only TFs in TAPscan classifications
tapscan_tfs <- lapply(families, function(x) x[x$TAP_class %in% "TF", ])

# Get TF counts per TAPscan subfamily
tapscan_counts <- get_tf_counts(
    tapscan_tfs, scheme = "TAPscan", level = "subfamily"
)
head(SummarizedExperiment::assay(tapscan_counts))
```

As additional examples, here is how you can get TF counts per Plant-TFClass 
superclass, and per TFClass class:

```{r get_tf_counts_planttfclass}
# Get TF counts per Plant-TFClass superclass
superclass_counts <- get_tf_counts(
    families, scheme = "PlantTFClass", level = "superclass"
)
SummarizedExperiment::assay(superclass_counts)

# Get TF counts per TFClass class
tfclass_counts <- get_tf_counts(families, scheme = "TFClass", level = "class")
head(SummarizedExperiment::assay(tfclass_counts))
```

Cool, huh? In real-world analyses, once you have TF counts per family in 
multiple species obtained with `get_tf_counts()`, 
you can try to find associations between TF counts and
eco-evolutionary aspects or traits of each species (e.g., higher frequencies of
a stress-related TF family in a species that inhabits a stressful environment).

# Curated human TFs

The human TFs were manually curated by experts [@lambert2018human], who
examined each candidate protein and the evidence for its sequence-specific
DNA binding. This curated list is more accurate than TFs identified from
the human proteome based on DBDs only (e.g., several chromatin regulators 
and RNA-binding proteins contain DBD-like domains), so we provide it in 
the data set `human_tfs`, with TFs already classified with the CIS-BP and 
TFClass schemes. 

```{r human_tfs}
data(human_tfs)
head(human_tfs)

# Number of TFs per DNA-binding assessment
table(human_tfs$TF_assessment)
```

TFClass classifications were obtained directly from TFClass for TFs in 
TFClass (column *TFClass_source*), and inferred from CIS-BP families for
other TFs. As `human_tfs` has the same columns as the output of 
`classify_tfs()` for the CIS-BP and TFClass schemes, you can pass it to
`get_tf_counts()` together with your own classifications (e.g., 
`list(Human = human_tfs, Species2 = ...)`).

```{r human_tfs_counts}
# Count human TFs per TFClass superclass
human_counts <- get_tf_counts(
    list(Human = human_tfs), scheme = "TFClass", level = "superclass"
)
SummarizedExperiment::assay(human_counts)
```
